probes.name: router_health
probes.direction: Is anything listening on the product endpoint at all? Everything after this is meaningless if it is not, so it runs first and short-circuits the rest.

probes.name: worker_registered
probes.direction: The router is up but is any worker attached? This is the failure that looks like a slow server: the router answers `/health`, accepts a completion, and the request then queues or 500s with nothing in the router log. Measured upstream in the same shape — sglang-router calls `/get_server_info` during `discover_metadata` with a hard-coded 10 s timeout, and a worker whose metadata call times out is **never registered** while everything else looks healthy.

probes.name: mode_readback
probes.direction: Was the deployment shape actually achieved? `mix` is selected by **omitting** a flag, so the launch command is not evidence of it. This is the router's independent reading; `check_deploy_kit` separately requires the worker's own.

probes.name: model_identity
probes.direction: Is the model registered under its published name, or under the filesystem path it was loaded from? The second is what a caller copies into every request, so it travels much further than the host it came from. It is also the single most common cause of a mysterious 400 against a healthy server: the model id the client sends does not exist on the server.

probes.name: engine_generation_ready
probes.direction: **The one probe that separates "the HTTP layer answers" from "the model can generate".** `/health`, `/v1/models` and `/get_model_info` do not go through the scheduler's ZMQ path, so all three keep answering while generation is wedged; `/health_generate` runs an actual generation. A deployment that passes the four probes above and fails this one is up, is serving, and will hang the first real request.

probes.name: engine_model_info
probes.direction: Did the engine load the checkpoint the kit says it did? Discriminates a server that is healthy and serving **the wrong weights** — which no latency or health probe can see and which silently invalidates every number every later stage produces.

probes.name: engine_server_info
probes.direction: Were the launch arguments the kit documents the ones the server is actually running? Read back rather than asserted — the flags a later stage needs to match (tp size, context length, graph capture) are here.

probes.name: completion_nonstreaming
probes.direction: A real answer comes back through the **router**, not only from the engine port, and it finished on its own. Discriminates three faults that all present as a working server: a reasoning parser that eats `content` and leaves it **empty** while the request still succeeds; a token budget too small for a reasoning preamble, which returns `finish_reason: "length"`; and a router that accepts but does not forward. **What it does NOT check, corrected after this text claimed otherwise:** it does not look at what the content *says*. The assertions below are `stop`, non-empty, and a model id that is not a path — so the inverse of the first fault passes. Measured on rung 1: with no `--reasoning-parser`, Qwen3.6-27B returned `finish_reason: stop`, `reasoning_tokens: 0`, and a `content` beginning *"Here's a thinking process:"* — 157 tokens of chain-of-thought in the field a caller reads as the answer. Every assertion here passed it. **`nonempty: true` was written against a parser that removes too much and is structurally blind to one that removes nothing.** The fix needs a bar nobody has measured yet; `todo.md` **T21** carries the proposed shape and the one measurement that would set it. Until then, read a pass here as "the product path returned something" and not as "the product path returned an answer".

probes.name: completion_streaming
probes.direction: The streaming path is **different code** from the non-streaming one, and every benchmark downstream of this stage measures TTFT and ITL over it. A deployment whose non-streaming path works and whose stream never terminates is one that passes every probe above and produces no measurement at all.

probes.name: context_limit_refused
probes.direction: Is the context length the server enforces the one the kit documents? A server started with a smaller window than the kit claims accepts every short request and truncates or refuses the long ones — visible here and nowhere else in this validator. **And the researched trap this row exists for:** SGLang's OpenAI-compatible endpoint returns HTTP **400** for a context overflow when `stream: false`, but HTTP **200 carrying an error payload** when `stream: true` — where vLLM returns 400 for both. A checklist that gates on the status line alone therefore reports a streaming failure as a success. So this probe is sent **twice**, once each way, and the streaming half is judged on the body.
probes.body_head: {"object":"error","message":"The input (39331 tokens) is longer than the model's context length (32768 tokens).","type":"BadRequestError","param":null,"code":400}

probes.name: metrics_exposed
probes.direction: Can a later stage tell **saturated** from **broken**? A server can pass every health probe while requests sit in the scheduler queue, and the two look identical from the outside. `sglang:num_queue_reqs`, `sglang:cache_hit_rate` and the latency histograms are what distinguish them, and they are also what m2 reads.
